stances.claim: Both sides cheered the RH decision because the emphatic fallo declared the RH Law NOT UNCONSTITUTIONAL except for eight specific provisions struck down -- giving pro-RH respondents enforcement of family-planning access, information, and school education, while giving pro-life petitioners the Court's assent that contraception pervades the entire law and unwavering protection of the fertilized ovum.
stances.rhetorical_move: both-sides-victory framing via fallo-vs-doctrine analytical split

stances.claim: Pro-life major victory: the Court held that a zygote is a human organism and that the life of a new human being commences at the scientifically well-defined moment of conception, that is, upon fertilization -- explicitly rejecting Lagman's theory that life begins at implantation, and relying on Charter framers Villegas and Davide's ConCom deliberations.

Pro-RH major victory: with the lifting of the SQAO, the RH Law may now be used as an enhancement measure to fortify and make effective the current laws on contraception, women's health, and population control -- including modern family-planning access for the poor and marginalized, mandatory health-provider information on the full range of methods, and mandatory school reproductive-health education.

Other pro-life victories include conscientious-objector protection (no force to use or prescribe contraceptives, no force to refer to other providers -- to compel would force them to do indirectly what they cannot do directly, violating non-coercion), with a life-threatening exception (right to life has preference over right to religious belief), and the striking down of spousal absolute-authority + barring-other-spouse + foregoing-parental-consent-for-minors provisions.

notable_anecdotes: The both-sides-jubilant framing -- 'I understood why both sides were jubilant' after reading the 106-page ponencia plus the separate opinions -- used as analytical lens for the entire column.
CJ Sereno's separate opinion noted as 'written in elegant and idiomatic Filipino' -- a rare CJP aesthetic-stylistic compliment on a colleague's prose in a national-language separate opinion.

Carpio's quoted formulation that the RH Law is replete with provisions embodying the policy to protect the fertilized ovum and afford it safe travel to the uterus for implantation -- the most lyrical doctrinal coinage Panganiban quotes from the decision.

Villegas-and-Davide-from-ConCom-deliberations citation -- using framers' intent to anchor the fertilization-not-implantation doctrine -- a rare original-intent move CJP makes more characteristic of US conservatives like Scalia.
The do-indirectly-what-they-cannot-do-directly principle as the linchpin of conscientious-objector protection -- among the column's sharpest doctrinal phrasings.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains why both sides instantly cheered the Imbong v. Ochoa (April 8 2014) decision on the RH Law (RA 10354). After reading the 106-page ponencia by J. Jose Catral Mendoza plus separate opinions from CJ Sereno (in elegant idiomatic Filipino), Justices Carpio, Leonardo-De Castro, Brion, Del Castillo, Abad, Reyes, Perlas-Bernabe, and Leonen, he understood why both camps were jubilant. The pro-RH respondents cheered the emphatic fallo: the RH Law is NOT UNCONSTITUTIONAL except for eight specific provisions declared UNCONSTITUTIONAL; the Status Quo Ante Order was LIFTED, enabling immediate enforcement; and the law may now serve as an enhancement measure to fortify and make effective the current laws on contraception, women's health, and population control -- including modern family-planning access for the poor and marginalized, mandatory health-provider information on the full range of methods, and mandatory school reproductive-health education. The pro-life petitioners cheered because the Court agreed that the whole idea of contraception pervades the entire RH Law and gave unwavering protection to the fertilized ovum: every human being enjoys the right to life, grounded on natural law, inherent and not dependent on particular law, custom, or belief. The Court -- while opting not to make any determination at this stage on when life begins -- held that the RH Law itself clearly mandates protection from the moment of fertilization, with Justice Carpio pointing out that the law is replete with provisions embodying the policy to protect the fertilized ovum and that it should be afforded safe travel to the uterus for implantation. Constitutional framers Villegas and Davide were cited from ConCom deliberations that when the Charter spoke of protecting life from the moment of conception, it referred to the moment when the ovum is fertilized by the sperm; the undeniable conclusion, per the Court, is that a zygote is a human organism and the life of a new human being commences at the scientifically well-defined moment of conception, upon fertilization -- rejecting Hon. Edcel Lagman's theory that life begins at implantation. Other pro-life victories: conscientious-objector health providers cannot be forced to use or prescribe contraceptives, nor to refer patients to other providers, because to compel them would force them to do indirectly what they cannot do directly, violating the principle of non-coercion enshrined in the Charter -- with a life-threatening exception where the right to life has preference over the right to religious belief. Also struck down were the provisions giving absolute authority to the spouse who would undergo a procedure and barring the other spouse from participating (endangering marriage and family for population reduction), and foregoing parental consent for minors.
